claims.text: High-temperature plastic deformation and toughness in fusion plasma-facing alloys are governed by competition between dislocation-driven strain hardening and diffusion-mediated dynamic recovery.
The proposed initial state has a refined, controlled grain size and precipitate distribution produced without prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Flow-stress data from high-temperature testing can be used to determine activation energies for plastic deformation.
Dynamic recovery is mediated by diffusion of point defects and dislocations.
Dynamic recovery reduces dislocation pile-up and moderates strain hardening.
At high temperatures, thermal energy facilitates atomic diffusion that enables dynamic recovery.
Dynamic recovery relieves dislocation stresses generated during plastic deformation.
Dynamic recovery enhances ductility and toughness.
Annealed samples will have lower flow stress than unannealed samples tested under identical conditions.
Annealed samples will have altered and potentially enhanced toughness relative to unannealed samples.
Annealing will shift the measured activation energy for deformation toward values characteristic of diffusion.
The activation energies for plastic deformation of CoCrFeMnNi can be close to its weighted diffusion activation energy.
The as-fabricated baseline has higher flow stress because it undergoes less pronounced dynamic recovery.
Diffusion is sufficiently active to control the proposed response typically within 600–1000 °C.
Recrystallization, grain-boundary sliding, or deformation twinning may dominate outside the proposed conditions or in other alloy systems.
The magnitude of changes in flow stress and toughness depends on composition, grain size, deformation conditions, and concurrent microstructural transformations.
Reduced dislocation density or rearranged dislocation structures would constitute microstructural evidence of enhanced dynamic recovery.
